basic_identification.name: Scene documentation gap
basic_identification.originator: Systemic gap. No single organization addresses this. Partial responses: Art Dubai (Global South platforming), Venice Biennale 2024 (Adriano Pedrosa's indigenous focus), Tezos community events (Tibum residency for Global South artists), Right Click Save (geographic coverage in A-Z), local collectives (e.g., SocialCryptoDAO from Tezos/Brazil ecosystem)
basic_identification.year: Ongoing. Recognized acutely since 2021 when NFT boom revealed how geographically concentrated the visible digital art field is
basic_identification.key_url: No single URL — this is a structural absence
basic_identification.geography: The gap IS geographic. Undocumented scenes exist in: Southeast Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, Central Asia, Eastern Europe, the Middle East (outside UAE art fair circuit), and small/mid-size cities globally. Documented scenes are concentrated in: New York, London, Berlin, Los Angeles, Paris, and select crypto-hub cities

core_ideas.core_claim: Local and regional digital art scenes are undocumented and invisible to the broader field. The field suffers from geographic blindness, seeing only what is visible through English-language platforms, major art fairs, and well-funded institutions. Entire communities of practice exist outside this visibility radius, producing work, building local infrastructure, and developing aesthetic approaches that never enter the global discourse.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Digital art should theoretically transcend geographic barriers — the internet enables global distribution. But in practice, visibility is determined by platform algorithms, language barriers, institutional access, and network effects that reproduce the same geographic concentrations as traditional art. A generative artist in Lagos and one in Berlin use the same tools (p5.js, Processing) but have vastly different access to visibility, funding, and community recognition.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: The attention economy concentrates visibility in already-visible locations. Platform algorithms favor content that already has engagement, creating feedback loops that amplify established scenes and suppress emerging ones. English-language content dominates search results and social media feeds. The attention economy is structurally geographic even when the medium is not.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Documenting scenes is deeply intention-aligned. It serves the field's need for accurate self-knowledge, diverse perspectives, and equitable representation. The gap represents a failure to act on declared values of inclusivity and global representation — the field says it values diversity but has not built the infrastructure to see it.

market_economics.revenue_model: Scene documentation has no revenue model. It is an unfunded public good. Occasional documentation happens through: art fair publications (Art Dubai catalogues), biennale programs, academic research, journalist travel grants, and community-funded initiatives. None of these are systematic or sustained.
market_economics.market_position: Infrastructure — outside the market but essential to market diversification. Undocumented scenes cannot participate in global markets. Documentation is a precondition for market access.
market_economics.price_range: Not applicable directly. However, the documentation gap correlates with price disparity: artists in undocumented scenes typically sell for significantly less than equivalent work from documented scenes, when they can sell at all.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Mixed signals. Art Dubai 2025 expanded Global South representation. The ArtReview Power 100 in 2024 included over 40 African, diaspora, and Global South figures. Venice Biennale 2024 prioritized indigenous and underrepresented artists. These are positive signals at the institutional level. But grassroots scene documentation remains underfunded and unsystematic. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: Undocumented scenes have predominantly local collector bases, if any. Crypto-native collectors occasionally discover non-Western artists through Tezos or other low-cost chains, but this is algorithmic and unsystematic. Traditional collector demographics remain heavily North American and European. [uncertain]
market_economics.sustainability: The documentation gap is self-reinforcing. Undocumented scenes cannot attract funding because funders do not know they exist. Without funding, documentation does not happen. Without documentation, funders remain unaware. Breaking this cycle requires intentional investment in documentation infrastructure.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Documentation requires: translation services, local correspondents/contributors, multilingual publication platforms, travel budgets, interview and documentation protocols, and structured databases that can accommodate non-English metadata. Most existing platforms lack these capabilities.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: AI translation tools could help bridge language barriers in documentation. AI-assisted transcription and summarization could reduce documentation costs. However, AI tools also risk flattening cultural specificity and imposing English-language conceptual frameworks on non-Western practice. The relationship is promising but requires careful design.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Scenes are living, evolving entities. Documentation must capture not just current state but temporal dynamics — formation, growth, transformation, decline. Static snapshots are insufficient. The field needs ongoing, updateable scene documentation, not one-time surveys.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Different scenes develop different aesthetic vocabularies rooted in local cultural, political, and material conditions. The documentation gap means these vocabularies are invisible to the global field. English-language critical frameworks are imposed on diverse practices, flattening local specificity. Scene documentation must include vocabulary documentation — how practitioners in each scene describe their own work.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Commons over capture (scene knowledge should be shared, not enclosed). Infrastructure over spectacle (documentation is invisible foundational work). Openness over enclosure (documentation should be publicly accessible). Collective over individual (scenes are collective phenomena, not individual achievements).

infrastructure_governance.openness: The gap itself is about closure — scenes are enclosed within local contexts without pathways to broader visibility. Addressing the gap requires radical openness: multilingual documentation, open data, public access to scene records.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: No governance model exists because no systematic documentation infrastructure exists. Individual documentation efforts are governed by their creators (journalists, researchers, curators). Any future documentation infrastructure would need to balance global coordination with local autonomy.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Critical concern. Scene documentation must be controlled by the scenes themselves, not extracted by external researchers or institutions. The risk of extractive documentation — outsiders documenting scenes for external audiences without local benefit — is high. Data sovereignty must be built into any documentation framework.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Zero. Existing documentation (scattered articles, social media posts, local websites) is not structured, tagged, or interoperable. No standard exists for scene documentation that could enable comparison, mapping, or integration across regions.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Absent. Existing scene documentation (social media posts, ephemeral web content, local event records) is highly vulnerable to loss. No institution systematically preserves scene-level documentation for digital art.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Absent but critically needed. Any documentation framework must include consent mechanisms for scenes and individuals documented. Scenes should be able to control how they are represented, what information is shared, and who has access. This is especially important for scenes in politically sensitive contexts.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: The traditional art world has extensive infrastructure for scene documentation: biennales, art fairs, gallery networks, critical publications, curatorial travel. But this infrastructure is concentrated in a small number of cities and institutional networks. Digital art's scene documentation gap mirrors and extends traditional art world geographic biases.
field_position.what_it_enables: Scene documentation enables: global field awareness, cross-pollination between distant communities, equitable representation in institutional programming, funding directed toward underserved regions, and the development of diverse aesthetic approaches.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Systematic methodology. Multilingual capacity. Sustained funding. Local correspondents embedded in scenes. Structured data formats for scene documentation. Integration with broader field intelligence systems. Mechanisms for scenes to self-document and contribute their own knowledge.
field_position.who_is_excluded: By definition, the excluded are the undocumented: digital art practitioners and communities in the Global South, non-English-speaking regions, and small/mid-size cities. Artists without platform presence (no Twitter/X, no Instagram, no marketplace listings) are completely invisible. Communities that organize through local channels (WhatsApp groups, local forums, in-person meetups) rather than global platforms.
field_position.frontier_signal: Emerging awareness but minimal action. The 2024 ArtReview Power 100 shift toward Global South representation is a signal of changing awareness. Art Dubai's expansion is another signal. But grassroots digital art scene documentation remains unfunded and unsystematic. The gap is increasingly recognized but not yet addressed.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Currently: serendipity, personal networks, art fair visibility, occasional journalism. No systematic discovery mechanism for undocumented scenes. Platform algorithms do not surface geographically diverse content by default.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: The gap IS an attention failure. Undocumented scenes lack attention infrastructure: they are not indexed, not translated, not platformed. Addressing the gap requires building attention pathways that bypass algorithmic concentration effects.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Strongly intention-aligned. The field declares commitments to diversity, global representation, and equitable access. Scene documentation is the infrastructure that would make these commitments operational. Without it, they remain aspirational.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Potentially transformative. Systematic scene documentation would radically expand the field's shared knowledge, revealing practices, approaches, and communities currently invisible. This would be one of the highest-value commons contributions possible.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Neither — scenes are not currently tracked in any provenance system. But scene context is a crucial form of meaning provenance: knowing that an artist emerged from a specific local community, with specific influences and conditions, is essential to understanding their work.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Scenes operate on their own temporal cycles: formation, growth, peak activity, transformation or decline. These cycles are often out of sync with global art market cycles. Documentation must capture temporal dynamics, not just snapshots.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: This item IS about absence detection. The gap represents the field's inability to see what it does not see. Addressing it requires actively searching for what is missing — inverting the normal logic of documentation (which records what is present) to investigate what is absent.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence. Scene documentation should reveal the actual diversity of the field without forcing consensus about which scenes matter. Multiple valid ways of organizing digital art practice should coexist in a documentation framework.
coherence.contestability: High and necessary. Scenes are contested — who belongs, what characterizes the scene, where it begins and ends. Any documentation framework must allow for contested definitions and multiple perspectives on the same scene.
coherence.forkability: High. Scene documentation can be done by anyone with local knowledge. The barrier is resources, not permissions. Communities can self-document if given platforms, tools, and templates.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: A(DAI) should build scene documentation as a core intelligence function. Its sensing loop should actively scan for undocumented scenes using multilingual search, local correspondents, and community contribution pathways. A(DAI) should adopt the principle that geographic diversity is a data quality issue — a knowledge system that only sees London, New York, and Berlin is fundamentally incomplete. The scenes/ directory in the A(DAI) intelligence repo should be one of its most actively developed layers.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: A(DAI) should refuse extractive documentation — documenting scenes from the outside for external consumption without local benefit. It should refuse English-only documentation. It should refuse treating scenes as static categories rather than evolving communities. It should refuse the assumption that platform-visible activity represents the full scope of a scene.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: A(DAI) is a centralized knowledge system attempting to document distributed, local phenomena. The tension is between global coherence (structured, comparable, interoperable data) and local specificity (each scene has its own logic, vocabulary, and context). A(DAI) must hold this tension by designing flexible schemas that accommodate diversity without flattening it.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Minimal direct regulatory exposure. However, documentation of scenes in politically sensitive contexts (e.g., digital art communities in authoritarian regimes) raises safety concerns. GDPR and similar privacy regulations may apply to documentation of individuals within scenes. Data protection requirements vary by jurisdiction.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Scene documentation should be open access. Local contributions should be attributed to contributors. No intellectual property model is established for scene-level documentation.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Must be opt-in. Scenes and individuals should consent to documentation. Particularly important for communities in contexts where visibility could create risk. No framework currently exists for this.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: The visibility of scenes depends on platform access. Communities on Twitter/X, Instagram, and major marketplaces are partially visible. Communities organized through local platforms, messaging apps, or in-person gatherings are invisible to global observers. This platform dependency creates systematic bias in the field's self-knowledge.
ecosystem.network_effects: Strong negative network effects for undocumented scenes: the less visible a scene is, the less investment it attracts, making it less visible. Conversely, documented scenes attract more attention, funding, and institutional recognition, amplifying existing concentrations. Documentation infrastructure would reverse this dynamic.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: The 2022-2023 crash disproportionately affected undocumented scenes. Global South communities that entered the NFT ecosystem (particularly through Tezos and hic et nunc) lost market income when volumes collapsed. Without institutional fallback, many local communities fragmented. Post-crash: art fair platforming (Art Dubai, Venice) provides some institutional visibility, but grassroots scenes remain underdocumented.
